whatItDoes: Computes the voltage drop along a wire run for 12V, 24V, 120V, or 240V AC systems, single- or three-phase. Enter the current, the one-way length, the AWG, and the wire material (copper or aluminum); see the drop in volts and percent, plus a pass/fail against the recommended limit (3% for 12V/24V, 3% for 120V/240V single-phase, 5% for 240V three-phase).
whyItExists: Voltage drop is the silent killer of low-voltage systems. A wire that's 'thick enough' for the current can still cause motors to stall and LEDs to dim if the run is long. The recommended limit (typically 3% for low-voltage and 5% for three-phase mains) is what the NEC and most equipment manuals use. This calculator checks that limit instantly.
whoShouldUse: Solar installers sizing battery and panel cables, marine and RV electricians, off-grid and battery-backed-up electricians, audio / PA / lighting installers running long cable runs, and three-phase commercial electricians verifying feeder sizes.
useCases: Verify a 12V solar battery cable won't drop below 11.5V at the inverter
Size a 24V LED strip wire so the strip gets 23V+ at the far end
Confirm a 100ft 120V feeder doesn't drop below 116V under load
Check a 240V three-phase motor feeder stays within the 5% NEC guideline
Compare copper vs aluminum wire for the same run
instructions: Pick the system: 12V / 24V / 120V single / 240V single / 240V three-phase
Pick the wire material: copper or aluminum
Enter the load current in amps
Enter the one-way run length in feet (round-trip is computed automatically)
Pick the wire gauge from the AWG dropdown
Read the drop in volts and percent; green = within limit, red = too high
examples: 12V, 15A, 50ft, AWG 12 copper → 1.18V drop, 9.84% — exceeds 3%, use AWG 8
12V, 15A, 50ft, AWG 8 copper → 0.47V drop, 3.94% — still over 3%, use AWG 6
24V, 10A, 30ft, AWG 14 copper → 1.13V drop, 4.71% — exceeds 3%, use AWG 12
bestPractices: Use the 3% rule for 12V and 24V systems — they have the least headroom
For 120V/240V mains, NEC recommends ≤ 3% drop on the branch circuit and ≤ 5% total (feeder + branch)
If the calculator says 'over limit', go to a heavier gauge (lower AWG number) or split the run into shorter segments
Aluminum wire is ~1.54× more resistive than copper — go two AWG sizes heavier to match copper performance
For long DC runs (battery cables, solar), use the voltage-drop calculator plus a 25% safety margin on the current
commonMistakes: Entering the round-trip length instead of one-way (the calculator doubles it internally — entering 100ft round-trip gives 200ft total)
Choosing aluminum when the wire is actually copper (1.54× resistance difference is significant)
Ignoring the 3% / 5% recommended limit (the math is right, the system just won't work well)
Picking the wrong phase (single-phase vs three-phase — three-phase uses √3 in the formula)
Forgetting that wire resistance increases with temperature (values are at 20°C, hotter runs are worse)
faq: What's the recommended voltage-drop limit? — 3% for low-voltage (12V/24V) and 120V/240V single-phase branch circuits, 5% total (feeder + branch) for 240V three-phase. Below 3% is 'excellent'; 3-5% is 'acceptable'; over 5% means equipment may not work correctly.

Why does the formula double the length? — Current flows out on one conductor and back on the other. The total wire the current travels is L + L, so we use 2L. For three-phase, the formula is √3 × I × R × L (line-to-line voltage, line current).

Does the wire temperature matter? — Yes. The values shown are at 20°C. A wire in a hot attic (say 40°C) has ~1.08× the resistance. The calculator doesn't model this; for hot-environment runs, derate by 10-15% or use a heavier gauge.

What gauge do I need for a 100ft run at 12V / 30A? — Use the calculator with current=30, length=100, gauge=8 copper. The drop is ~6.28V (way too high). Try AWG 4: drop ~2.5V (4.2%, still over 3%). Try AWG 2: drop ~1.6V (2.7%, OK). So AWG 2 copper for 100ft at 30A, 12V.

Why does the calculator say 'over limit' but the equipment still works? — The recommended limits are conservative. Many loads (especially resistive ones like heaters) tolerate 5-10% drop without complaint. Sensitive electronics (CPUs, sensors, LED drivers) need the full 3%.
features: Pass/fail indicator (green = within limit, red = exceeds)
Recommended limit (3% for 12V/24V/120V/240V single, 5% for three-phase)
